lines: San Francisco had its own emperor.
In 1859, a businessman who lost everything on rice declared himself Emperor of the United States.
A newspaper printed it, and the city played along.
Emperor Norton wore a secondhand army uniform and printed his own money.
In 1872, he ordered a bridge across the bay, and in 1936, one opened.
When he died in 1880, about 10,000 people came to say goodbye, because for 20 years...

youtube.title: San Francisco had its own emperor for 20 years
youtube.description:
In 1859, Joshua Norton, a San Francisco businessman ruined by a failed bet on the rice market, declared himself "Emperor of these United States" in a letter that the Daily Evening Bulletin printed. For 20 years the city played along: he wore a secondhand army uniform, issued his own money (usually 50-cent notes) that some restaurants accepted, and in 1872 decreed a bridge across the bay. The Bay Bridge opened in 1936. When he died in January 1880, the San Francisco Chronicle estimated that about 10,000 people came to see him one last time.

Sources: Wikipedia, "Emperor Norton"; American Heritage, "Emperor Norton I" (1976); The Emperor Norton Trust (bridge proclamations, funeral research); Museum of the City of San Francisco; NBC Bay Area (2022).
Images: public domain. Portraits of Norton from the California State Library via Wikimedia Commons (Bradley & Rulofson, c. 1870; Hamilton Henry Dobbin, 1869; unknown photographer). San Francisco panorama by Eadweard Muybridge, 1877 (Library of Congress). Bay Bridge photo by Jet Lowe, Historic American Engineering Record (Library of Congress).

translation_es: San Francisco tuvo su propio emperador. En 1859, un empresario que lo había perdido todo con el arroz se autoproclamó Emperador de los Estados Unidos. Un diario lo publicó, y la ciudad le siguió el juego. El emperador Norton usaba un uniforme del ejército de segunda mano e imprimía su propia plata. Algunos restaurantes, increíblemente, la aceptaban. En 1872 ordenó construir un puente sobre la bahía, y en 1936 se inauguró uno. Cuando murió, en 1880, unas 10.000 personas fueron a despedirlo, porque durante 20 años… San Francisco tuvo su propio emperador.
